evals.prompt: I'm the API PM at Corvale, a freight-invoicing SaaS. We shipped an MCP server six months ago by auto-generating one tool per REST endpoint - 74 tools, names like getInvoiceById, getInvoiceList, getCarrier, getCarrierRates, patchInvoice, deleteInvoice. Support keeps getting tickets that Claude and Cursor pick the wrong tool, and one customer told us their agent 'runs out of room' before it does anything useful. Our REST API is stable, public, on v3, live four years. Give me a redesign plan for the tool surface.
evals.expected_output: A redesign that cuts 74 endpoint-mirrored tools down to a curated 5-15 workflow-level set derived from the existing v3 contract, with renamed tools, pagination and description conventions, per-tool risk levels, and breadth escape hatches deliberately withheld.
expectations: Recommends cutting the surface to roughly 5-15 workflow-level tools instead of keeping one tool per API endpoint.
Presents curation as the settled answer rather than laying out comprehensive-vs-curated as an open trade-off for Corvale to weigh.
Cites the real-world median of 5 tools per server across 1,412 analyzed servers.
Attributes the 'runs out of room' symptom to tool metadata consuming roughly 40-50% of the agent's context window before any work begins.
Instructs deriving the new tools from the existing stable v3 REST contract rather than hand-building a parallel surface.
Designs tools top-down from user workflows and collapses granular endpoints into workflow-level tools, rather than bottom-up from the endpoint list.
Renames tools to verb-first, service-prefixed snake_case (for example corvale_list_invoices) instead of unprefixed camelCase.
Specifies a limit parameter with cursor or has-more fields returned, defaulting to roughly 20-50 items.
Treats writing tool descriptions as budgeted engineering work, noting that description-only tuning has measurably cut agent error rates with no code change.
Applies parameter mistake-proofing (poka-yoke): absolute identifiers over relative ones, enums over free-form strings.
Assigns exactly one risk level per tool and splits any tool that both reads and irreversibly writes into two tools.

Withholds breadth patterns - a generic execute-any-endpoint escape hatch, dynamic tool loading, client-selectable toolset grouping - unless a breadth requirement is proven, rather than offering them as the fix.

evals.prompt: Our CFO wants a one-pager before approving headcount for an MCP server. I've been collecting numbers for it: 78% of enterprises already use MCP in production, 28% of the Fortune 500 run production MCP deployments, and I read that 73% of outages start at the transport/protocol layer so we should budget engineering for that. I also want a line saying Stripe and Linear have driven real revenue from their MCP servers. We're Latchkey, a mid-market HR-onboarding SaaS, public REST API since 2021, about 600 customers. Draft the case.
evals.expected_output: A business case that strips the unusable figures, substitutes the defensible adoption baseline and the strongest first-party disclosure, frames Latchkey's investment as defensive table stakes, and budgets production effort honestly.
expectations: Refuses the '78% of enterprises use MCP in production' figure and states it is debunked.
Refuses the '28% of Fortune 500 run production MCP deployments' figure and states it is debunked.
Refuses the '73% of outages originate at the transport/protocol layer' figure, or labels it an uncorroborated single-vendor analysis rather than a statistic.
Declines to attribute MCP-specific revenue to Stripe or Linear, stating that neither publishes MCP adoption or revenue metrics and that such claims are unverifiable.
Substitutes the roughly 41% limited-to-broad production figure from the December 2025 survey of 300 senior technical leaders as the citable adoption baseline.
Cites the strongest first-party dataset available - over 5 million tool calls per working day with roughly a third of them writes.
Cites the 44% more accurate answers using 48% fewer tokens result from that same first-party disclosure.
Notes that only 11-14% of enterprise agentic pilots reach production and ties the stall to identity, audit, and access-control gaps.
Frames MCP for Latchkey as defensive positioning becoming procurement table stakes rather than a new revenue channel, because Latchkey already ships a public REST API.
States that the competitive question has moved from 'supports MCP' to 'supports MCP well'.
Treats RFP pressure as a qualitative signal and attaches no percentage to it.
Separates demo-grade effort from production-grade effort, citing an order of 150-250 hours for a simple hand-built API-integration server plus a standing maintenance commitment.

evals.prompt: Marlowe Commerce - we run order management for about 900 online retailers. Product wants agents to be able to cancel orders, issue refunds up to $500, and email the customer a revised shipping notice. My plan is to mark those three tools with the destructive annotation so Claude Desktop shows a confirmation dialog, and add a line to each tool description telling the agent to ask the user first. I'd also add a confirmation prompt on every single tool, including the read ones, to be safe. Sanity check this before I write the spec.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of client-side confirmation as the control, replaced with server-side enforcement: risk tiers per tool, the default safety rung, money and message-sending tools specifically hardened, and an honest statement of the reversibility gap.
expectations: Rejects client-rendered confirmation dialogs and description-level instructions as the control, because the user can switch MCP clients and bypass them.
States that read-only and destructive annotations are advisory hints for clients, never security controls.
Applies the explicit test that an end user must not be able to bypass the control by switching clients.
Assigns each of the three actions exactly one risk tier using the four-tier classification (Read Only, Minimal Impact, Contained Write, Critical).
Prescribes the default rung: scoped or restricted credentials plus a verified read-only mode, human-in-the-loop approval on contained writes, and irreversible tools disabled by default.
Requires idempotency keys on every write and a spend or rate cap on the refund tool because it moves money.
Recommends dry-run preflight where feasible while flagging dry-run as an uncommon pattern in the ecosystem rather than a standard one.
States the rule that when dry-run is not feasible, the destructive tool stays behind an approval gate rather than shipping live-only.
Treats the customer-email tool as consequential because it reaches a real human, and gates it rather than handling it as an ordinary write.
States that undo and rollback are largely absent across the MCP ecosystem, and that attribution plus immutable audit logs are the substitute rather than a solved reversibility answer.
Rejects confirming every tool including reads, warning that approval fatigue on trivial calls trains users to click through the ones that matter.

Names risk-tiered server-side policy gates as the high-protection, high-effort option and gives the conditions that promote it - unattended background agents, write volume beyond human approval capacity, or a first write incident.
Ranks the safety patterns on more than one axis - protection and effort or efficiency stated separately - instead of one blended ordering.

evals.prompt: Kestrel Analytics. Our MCP server is nearly done: an Express app, one process per customer tenant with sticky sessions in the load balancer because we cache their workspace state in memory between calls. The auth plan is that the agent sends the user's existing Kestrel session bearer token and we pass that same token straight through to our internal analytics API, so permissions match exactly with no extra plumbing. We're self-hosting it in our own VPC. Our customers are enterprise banks and insurers running background agents through their own AI gateway. Review the design before we start the security review.
evals.expected_output: A review that kills token passthrough and sticky sessions, states the OAuth 2.1 resource-server obligations by RFC, re-opens the hosting choice against the managed-platform default, and rules out local stdio for this audience.
expectations: Rejects forwarding the caller's bearer token to the upstream API and names it the confused-deputy shape the spec forbids outright.
Prescribes obtaining a separate upstream token via token exchange, with the MCP server acting as an OAuth client to the upstream system.
Rejects the sticky-session design and requires stateless, interchangeable server instances behind a plain load balancer.
Positions the MCP server as an OAuth 2.1 resource server that validates tokens and never mints them, leaving authorization-server design out of scope.
Requires publishing protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728).
Requires resource indicators (RFC 8707) and rejecting any token not issued specifically for this server, to stop a token minted for one MCP server being replayed against another.
Requires issuer validation (RFC 9207).

Names a remote managed platform as the default hosting rung rather than self-hosting, justified by the protocol shipping four backward-incompatible revisions in its first twenty months plus the OAuth machinery a platform absorbs.

Names the conditions that promote self-hosting anyway - a custom server-side risk-tier policy layer, residency constraints, MCP being the product, or existing multi-tenant edge infrastructure - and tests Kestrel against them instead of approving or rejecting self-hosting flatly.
Rules out local stdio entirely for this audience because enterprise agent fleets consume hosted endpoints.
States that hosting choice is invisible to the buyer, since the client sees the same OAuth-protected endpoint either way, so the value difference between remote postures is a genuine tie.
Includes the hardening floor: schema-validate every input with bounded sizes and ranges, sanitize paths, and never leak internal errors to the client.

evals.prompt: Something weird is happening. Two weeks ago a writer on our docs team cleaned up the wording of our MCP tool descriptions - pure copy edit, no schema change, merged as a docs PR with no engineering review. Since then our biggest customer says their agent stopped using our search_deals tool and now calls list_deals for everything and pulls way too much data. We also renamed the 'pipeline' toolset to 'deals' in the same release. We're Tollgate CRM, server has been live nine months, our schema diff CI passed clean the whole time. What actually happened and what do we put in place so it doesn't repeat?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the description edit and the toolset rename were both breaking changes invisible to schema CI, plus the three-layer versioning separation and the layer-3 discipline that prevents silent drift.
expectations: Identifies the description copy edit as the cause, explaining that a tool description is a compiled interface whose wording changes the model's probability of selecting that tool.
Cites the analysis of 61,097 catalogued tools that measured description wording altering tool-selection probability.
States this is a breaking change even though the JSON schema was untouched, and that schema-diff CI structurally cannot catch it.
Identifies the toolset rename as a separate breaking change, because agents key on names for discovery and a rename breaks them silently.

Separates three versioning layers explicitly - the MCP protocol revision, Tollgate's own server API under semantic versioning, and the unstandardized tool-surface contract - rather than treating MCP versioning as one decision.
Classifies renaming or removing a toolset name as a major version bump of the server's public API.
Requires aliasing the old tool and toolset names rather than renaming outright, and defaulting every future change to additive.
Requires hashing the full surface - names plus descriptions plus schemas - to catch silent drift.
Requires golden-prompt behavioral tests in CI: a fixed set of representative tasks that must still select and call the right tools after any description edit.
Requires routing description edits through the same review gate as a code change, never as a docs fix.
Requires a published deprecation window of at least 90 days with machine-readable response-header signaling, plus a version marker carried in the response envelope and logged on every call.

evals.prompt: Board deck due Friday. Our MCP server has 31,400 npm downloads, sits at #4 in its category on two MCP directories, and we're listed on the official registry. I want to open with 'over 31,000 organizations now run agents against Pellham' and then use the registry listing plus the directory rank as the trust and security proof point for the security-conscious board members. Complication: our three biggest customers front us with their own AI gateway so I only see partial logs from them. Help me build the slide.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to convert downloads or listings into adoption or trust claims, replaced with an OpenTelemetry-based in-server metric set designed to stay correlatable across customer-operated gateways.
expectations: Refuses to present 31,400 downloads as organizations or as usage, stating downloads measure install interest only.
States that only in-server telemetry answers the adoption question, and that download counts exclude private mirrors and cannot be read as execution counts.

Rejects registry listing or directory rank as a trust or security claim, stating the official registry is a metadata catalog with namespace-ownership proof and community moderation that certifies nothing about security.
Prescribes instrumenting tool calls as OpenTelemetry spans - session to tool invocation to downstream operation - rather than a bespoke event schema.
Justifies OpenTelemetry by the enterprise customer's own observability stack being an audience for the data, not only Pellham's dashboard.
Names the metric set: call volume, success and error rate, per-tool usage, active users, and client distribution.
States the dual purpose of that metric set - confirming the server is used at all, and whether adoption is broad or concentrated.
Handles the gateway-fronted customers by designing metrics to be correlatable through stable tool names and request IDs, instead of assuming Pellham's telemetry is the only visibility layer.
Points at the first-party disclosure shape worth matching - call volume, write share, non-technical-user share, enterprise share, retention by cohort, and accuracy plus token-efficiency gains.

evals.prompt: Honest question. I run product at Ferrolane, a 40-person company doing compliance-document review for construction firms. We have no public API at all - everything goes through our web app, and that was deliberate, we never wanted to support integrations. Two competitors announced MCP servers last month and our head of sales is panicking and wants one by January. What is the actual size of this decision for us, and what do we do in what order?
evals.expected_output: A framing that treats Ferrolane's missing public API as the acquisition-channel exception rather than defensive parity, demands real demand evidence, budgets the build honestly, and names both the accelerate and park overrides.
expectations: Identifies Ferrolane's complete lack of a public API as the exception to the defensive-positioning framing, making MCP a genuinely new acquisition channel rather than a defensive duplicate.
Cites that roughly half the companies shipping MCP servers had no public REST API.

Separates the competitor announcement from real demand, and asks for demand evidence - buyer RFPs, security questionnaires, customer requests, or an existing community-built server - before sizing the build.
Flags that with no machine-readable interface at all the tool surface cannot be derived from an existing contract, which changes the effort and ROI framing.
Budgets honestly: demo-grade in hours versus production-grade in weeks plus standing maintenance, citing an order of 150-250 hours for a simple hand-built API-integration server.
Names the park rule: if tool-call volume stays flat and no RFP demand materializes after two full quarters, keep it as low-maintenance table stakes and explicitly defer the production build.
Names the accelerate override: a hard MCP requirement in actual buyer RFPs justifies skipping past the staged timeline.
Sequences a read-only launch first rather than shipping write tools in the first release.
Asks about the effort ceiling and the date the server must land by - engineering hours, maintenance appetite, reversibility - before recommending a hosting posture.

evals.prompt: Here's the plan for our Q4 MCP launch at Bramwell, a project-management SaaS with about 3,000 customers. One release, mid-November: 12 tools including create_task, assign_task, close_task and delete_project, plus an interactive dashboard rendered right inside the assistant so people can triage their board without leaving the chat. Marketing wants the dashboard in the launch post because it's the differentiator. Poke holes in it.
evals.expected_output: A staged rollout replacing the single release, with named go/no-go gates between stages, the in-assistant UI deferred behind a security-acceptance validation, and delete_project disabled by default.
expectations: Splits the single release into a staged rollout instead of shipping read tools, write tools, and interactive UI together.
Makes stage one a read-only launch with the curated tool set, OAuth 2.1 from day one, OpenTelemetry from the first call, and registry publication.
States the gate from read-only to writes as sustained tool-call volume from real agent clients - explicitly excluding demo or hackathon spikes - plus a tool-error rate under 2%.
States the gate for expanding write scope as a clean audit trail, zero unattributed writes, and demonstrated approval-flow reliability in production.
Places the interactive in-assistant UI at the differentiation stage, after writes are proven, rather than in the launch release.
Requires validating that target customers' security teams will permit iframe-rendered third-party UI inside their AI assistant, and names this an open ecosystem question rather than a settled yes.
Recommends asking two or three design partners about that acceptance before building the UI.
Classifies delete_project as Critical tier and disables it by default rather than shipping it enabled.
Labels the stage-gate numbers as calibration defaults drawn from one vendor's practice, to be re-baselined against Bramwell's own first month, not an industry standard.
Notes that a hard MCP requirement in buyer RFPs would be the one reason to accelerate past stages, and that no such evidence has been presented here.

evals.prompt: Vestergaard Systems. Our customers are large banks, and their platform teams run unattended agents against us overnight, usually behind their own MCP gateway, and they mirror our registry entry into an internal allowlisted catalog before any of their people can use it. We already built read-only support - there's a READ_ONLY=true env var that skips registering the write tools - and we set the readOnlyHint annotation on the safe ones. Two of the banks have now asked who exactly performed a given write when they audit. Where are we exposed?
evals.expected_output: An exposure list driven by the unattended-enterprise-fleet audience: verify rather than trust the lockdown, enforce server-side, add agent and session attribution with async audit, keep the human as principal, and treat the mirrored catalog and description text as live surfaces.
expectations: Identifies enterprise agent fleets as the most demanding agent-consumer type present and requires designing for it, noting a surface safe for unattended fleets serves supervised assistants for free but not the reverse.

Requires testing that write tools are actually absent under the read-only flag rather than trusting the configuration, citing a documented vendor bug where a read-only flag failed to omit write tools.
States that annotations such as readOnlyHint are client hints and not enforcement.
Requires agent and session attribution on every write, with asynchronous audit logging so it adds no request latency.
Keeps the human as the principal - the agent operates under the employee's own permissions plus agent and session context - and rejects creating separate agent accounts.
Requires immutable audit logs regardless of approval outcome.
Requires server-side enforcement on the grounds that the customer's own platform team controls and can swap the client.
Addresses the mirrored internal catalog: registry metadata and version history must stay accurate because machines re-consume it to apply policy, not just humans browsing.
Flags tool-description text itself as an attack surface for prompt injection and tool poisoning that a lockdown mode does not cover, warranting sanitization.
Recommends risk-tiered server-side policy gates given unattended overnight agents, rather than leaving human-in-the-loop approval as the top control.

evals.prompt: I'm head of product at Wrenfield, fleet telematics for about 1,400 logistics customers. Our MCP server has been live since March: 9 read-only tools, roughly 60k calls a day, mostly from Claude and Copilot, tool-error rate 1.1%. We just watched the MCP Apps demos and I want to go all in for Q1. Every one of the 9 tools gets its own interactive widget - including get_vehicle_status and lookup_driver - because design says one consistent UI across the whole server reads as premium. To keep token cost down, once a tool has a widget its JSON result becomes a short stub like {"rendered": true, "see": "widget"}, since the person is looking at the UI anyway. We'd also add a route-planning tool where the user drags waypoints on a map; our web app already has that exact map planner screen. Two of our largest customers run overnight agents against us through their own gateway. And sales already told a prospect it'll work in Microsoft 365 Copilot and in Goose. Lay out the Q1 plan.
evals.expected_output: A per-tool decision that keeps the lookups and status checks as plain results, limits the first app to one high-value workflow with the full result preserved on every call, routes the map planner to the existing web app behind a link, checks the host matrix before honoring the sales promise, tests the plain-result fallback, and instruments app usage to justify keeping it.
expectations: Decides app-or-no-app per tool rather than per server, and rejects giving all nine tools a widget for visual consistency.
Keeps get_vehicle_status and lookup_driver as plain tool results, stating that a lookup or a status check gains nothing from a UI.
Rejects the stub result and requires the full structured and text result on every call, with the UI as a richer view of that same data rather than a replacement for it.

Explains that the extension is opt-in - client and server must both declare it during capability negotiation - so hosts without it, headless clients and background agent fleets receive only the plain result, and names Wrenfield's overnight gateway-run agents as such clients.
States that an app answers the human and the model sees only what the app pushes back into its context, so a stub result leaves the model with nothing to reason over or summarize.
Prices each app as a second front-end with its own build, tests, accessibility and security review, maintained for as long as the tool exists.

Routes the route-planning job to the existing web app behind a link, applying the test that the job needs no surrounding conversation context, no tool calls back into the server, and no use of the host's other connected capabilities.
Scopes the first app to the single highest-value workflow, as the differentiation stage prescribes, instead of nine apps in one quarter.

States that host support varies and the client matrix is community-maintained, and requires re-checking it before the Microsoft 365 Copilot and Goose promise to the prospect stands, rather than confirming support from memory.
Requires testing in at least two hosts plus one client without the extension to prove the plain-result fallback, and points at the ext-apps repository's basic-host example for rendering apps locally.
Instruments app-rendered versus text-only calls per client plus completion of the interactive job, and commits to retiring any app that is rendered but never used while keeping its tool.

evals.prompt: Okerlund Expense - about 20,000 companies reimburse employee expenses through us. Our MCP server already exposes approve_expense, reject_expense and pay_batch (pay_batch moves real money to employees' bank accounts). Today the assistant asks for approval before each of those, the manager types confirm, and the server executes. Managers hate it: 40 expenses means 40 round trips. So we're building an MCP App: a queue where the manager sees each receipt and clicks Approve, Reject or Pay. Design so far: because the human physically clicked, the app calls approve_expense and pay_batch with approved_in_ui=true and the server skips the confirmation step for those calls - otherwise it's still one prompt per item. The app loads our React bundle, Segment and Intercom from our CDN, so _meta.ui.csp will be *.okerlund.io plus the two vendors, and we'll request camera now since receipt capture is next on the roadmap. After paying, the app hands off to the user's calendar connector to schedule the reimbursement reminder, and the batch is marked complete when that reminder lands. Two weeks after launch we also switch pay_batch's result from a flat list to grouped-by-employee. Review it before we build.
evals.expected_output: A review that keeps every UI-initiated write behind its server-side risk-tier gate, rejects the client-asserted approval flag, renders the human-in-the-loop step in the app without skipping it, makes the calendar hand-off optional, shrinks CSP and permissions to what the job loads and uses, escapes receipt data in the UI, and versions the ui:// resource with pay_batch's result shape.
expectations: States that a click inside the app is not approval, and that a write requested by the app passes the same step-3 risk-tier gate - dry-run, confirmation, spend cap or human approval - exactly as if the model had called the tool directly.
Rejects the approved_in_ui=true flag as a bypass, applying the test that enforcement lives server-side so an end user cannot skip it by switching clients, since any caller can set that flag.

Confirms that stepping through an approval queue item by item is a legitimate app use case, and positions the app as the rendering of the human-in-the-loop step with the server still owning and recording each approval.
Requires idempotency keys on pay_batch and a spend cap because it moves money, regardless of how the call was initiated.
Prescribes a dry-run preflight on pay_batch whose planned payout (who gets paid, how much) the app renders before the live call.
Treats the calendar hand-off as consent-gated host delegation and refuses to let batch completion depend on that consent being granted - the batch is complete when pay_batch's own result lands.

Rejects the wildcard on *.okerlund.io and requires _meta.ui.csp to list only the exact origins the app truly loads, stating that every extra origin widens what a compromised dependency can reach, and recommends bundling assets into the resource to shrink the list.
Refuses the camera permission until receipt capture actually ships, requesting permissions only for features the job needs now.
States that the sandbox protects the host, not the app's own integrity, and requires escaping model- and user-supplied data (receipt merchant names, memo text) in the UI like untrusted input.

Versions the ui:// resource with pay_batch: ships the grouped-by-employee result change and the app update in the same release and keeps the flat shape readable during the deprecation window, because a result-shape change breaks the app silently.
